doc.title: Mat Domber interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Studio time and recording face to face
summary: Arbors books ten hours, two sessions, per CD and values musicians playing together.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: How much time in the studio do you usually feel you’re able to afford for these musicians? Do you give them guidelines for that?

We generally book ten hours, two five hour sessions. And normally that’s enough to produce one CD. If it runs over in time and if we have to work instead of until six o’clock at night and we have to go to eight or nine, that’s fine. The music is the thing. I always figure to myself when you amortize the additional costs over the lifetime of the music it becomes inconsequential.

Oh, that’s a good way to look at it. It’s also interesting that that’s really how jazz records used to be made too. They would do one or two sessions and get your album made, rather than with pop records sometimes they take months and months.

Well we don’t record the way some pop albums are recorded where you have a guitar player in California and a singer in New York and a bass player in Texas you know. And they all lay down their tracks and then somehow they get all mixed together and put together. We don’t do that. We like the synergy of having the musicians face to face playing together. We think that’s important.
